items.title: The Joliot-Curies made elements radioactive on demand in 1934
items.claim: In January 1934 Irène Joliot-Curie (daughter of Marie) and her husband Frédéric Joliot bombarded aluminium foil with alpha particles. After removing the source, the foil continued emitting radiation — they had created phosphorus-30, a radioactive isotope that does not occur in nature.

options.text: Until then, all known radioactive elements occurred naturally. The Joliot-Curies showed any element could potentially be made radioactive by nuclear bombardment, opening the field of artificial isotopes for medicine, research and weapons
It produced the first synthetic element
It was unrelated to their parents' work

items.reveal:
Alpha + aluminium-27 → phosphorus-30 + neutron. P-30 decays with a half-life of 2.5 minutes to silicon-30 by positron emission — discovered along the way.

The Joliot-Curies won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, sharing it as a couple as Marie and Pierre had done in 1903.

Fermi (Rome, 1934) extended the work using neutrons as projectiles, producing many new isotopes including (he claimed) transuranic elements. He had actually produced uranium fission products — discovered as such by Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner in 1938.

Irène died in 1956 of leukaemia, almost certainly from radiation exposure. Frédéric died in 1958 of liver disease, also linked to radiation. Two generations of Curie women died of their work.
items.why: Until 1934, radioactivity was a property of certain natural elements. After 1934, it was a tool — at the cost of the lives of those who developed it.

items.title: Endpoint and equivalence point are NOT the same
items.claim: Add NaOH to vinegar with phenolphthalein indicator. The pink colour appears when you've added 'enough' base — that's the endpoint. The equivalence point (exactly stoichiometric H+ matches OH-) is at pH 8.7, not pH 7, and the endpoint depends on the indicator you choose.
items.prompt: Why do you pick phenolphthalein specifically for a weak-acid + strong-base titration?

options.text: Phenolphthalein's transition range (pH 8.2-10.0) brackets the equivalence point of weak-acid + strong-base titrations and lies on the steepest part of the pH curve — so endpoint approximately equals equivalence point

items.reveal:
Titrating ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) with NaOH gives an equivalence point at pH ~8.7 — not 7. The conjugate base CH3COO- is itself slightly basic and shifts the equivalence point above neutral.

Phenolphthalein (8.2-10.0) brackets this and changes colour in the steep part of the pH jump. Methyl orange (3.1-4.4) would change colour FAR before the equivalence point and give a wrong concentration.

A strong-acid + strong-base titration has equivalence at pH 7 with a very steep jump — almost any indicator works. A weak-acid + weak-base titration has no sharp jump at all and is usually monitored with a pH meter, not an indicator.

Calibration of standards, indicator choice, and meniscus reading all contribute to accuracy of the recorded endpoint volume.
items.why: Titrations are presented as if indicator change marks the answer exactly. The match between indicator pKa and equivalence pH determines accuracy.

items.title: Strong and concentrated are completely different
items.claim: A 0.0001 M solution of hydrochloric acid is a strong acid but dilute. A 12 M solution of ethanoic acid is concentrated but weak. Strength and concentration are independent properties of an acid.
items.prompt: What does 'strong' actually mean for an acid?

options.text: It feels acidic on the tongue
It is fully dissociated into ions in water (Ka very large); concentration is just how much acid is dissolved per unit volume
It is sold in glass bottles

items.reveal:
Strong acids — HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4 — dissociate essentially 100 percent in water. [H+] equals the acid concentration.

Weak acids — CH3COOH, HCN, H2CO3, HF — only partially dissociate. Vinegar is about 1 M ethanoic acid but [H+] is only about 0.004 M; most molecules stay intact.

Very dilute HCl is still strong (fully dissociated) but has a low [H+] and a high pH near 7. Glacial ethanoic acid is very concentrated but most molecules are undissociated — pH only modestly below 7 until water is added.

pKa describes strength; molarity describes concentration. They are independent properties.
items.why: Strength and concentration are routinely conflated. They measure entirely different physical properties of an acid.
